name: Screen and apply to remote jobs with MrScraper, Gemini and Telegram

parameters.content:
# Screen and Auto-Apply to Remote Jobs from 4 ATS

## Who's it for
Job seekers who lose hours a week to the same three chores: searching several
job sites, researching each employer, and retyping the same application. It is
built for people applying across borders, where a posting's location and
language quietly decide whether applying is even possible.

## What it does
Fill one row in a Google Sheet: CV link, target roles, salary floor, skills.
Every few hours the workflow searches four applicant tracking systems, reads
roughly two thousand live openings, scores each against your CV, researches the
pay range and what employees say about the company, drafts the application, and
sends you one digest. Where the ATS allows it and you approve, the application
is submitted for you.

## How it works
**Discover.** MrScraper's Google SERP finds company job boards. Nobody
publishes a directory of these subdomains, so searching is the only way
to find them at all. One token per page.

**Read.** Every opening then comes from that ATS's own public JSON API
over plain HTTP, which costs nothing. Tokens go only where no API exists.

**Rank.** A Code node throws out anything not remote, written in a
language you do not read, or aimed at someone far more senior. Free, and
it means the model only ever looks at plausible candidates.

**Score.** Gemini reads each opening against your CV in small batches and
returns typed JSON: a score, what fits, what does not, and any hard
blocker such as a work permit you do not hold.

**Research.** MrScraper pulls the salary benchmark and what employees say
about the company from pages that publish no feed of any kind. Results
are cached by role and country, so the same lookup is never paid twice.

**Draft.** Gemini writes the cover letter and answers the screening
questions, using only what your CV and portfolio actually support.

**Deliver.** One Telegram digest. Openings on Recruitee are submitted for
you once you approve them; the rest arrive researched and one tap from
done.

## How to use
1. Add four credentials: **MrScraper**, **Google Gemini**, **Google Sheets**, and
   a **Telegram** bot.
2. Create a Google Sheet with three tabs named `job_profile`, `seen_jobs` and
   `salary_cache`, then paste its document id into the Google Sheets nodes.
3. Fill one row on `job_profile`: name, email, phone, a public link that serves
   your CV as a real PDF, target roles, locations, salary and key skills. A
   Google Drive share link will not work, because it returns a web page rather
   than the file.
4. Put your Telegram chat id in **Run Settings**.
5. Leave `DRY_RUN` on for the first run, it prepares everything and shows the
   exact payload without sending. Turn it off when the output looks right.
6. Tune `MIN_MATCH_SCORE`, `REMOTE_ONLY` and `ATS_DOMAINS` to taste.

**Costs 200 to 750 MrScraper tokens per run.** Search is a steady 20. The rest is
the salary and review extraction, so the total tracks how many openings clear the
filter and get researched.

**The approval buttons need a reachable URL.** Telegram sends the Approve link to
your phone, so `WEBHOOK_URL` has to point somewhere your phone can open. A public
tunnel works but free ephemeral ones expire mid-run; pointing `WEBHOOK_URL` at
your machine's LAN address and keeping the phone on the same network is simpler
and does not expire.

## Only Recruitee can be applied to automatically
All four ATS publish their listings openly, but only Recruitee exposes an
unauthenticated endpoint for creating a candidate. Lever, Ashby and Greenhouse
keep submission behind employer credentials, so those openings arrive fully
researched with answers drafted, one tap from done rather than automatic.

## It will not lie on your behalf
Real postings ask *"Are you fluent in Dutch?"* and *"Do you live within 50 km of
Amsterdam?"*, marked required. A model optimising for pass-rate would answer
yes. This one answers only from your CV, and any required question it cannot
honestly answer stops that submission. The application goes out under your real
name.

parameters.text:
=You are screening job openings for one specific applicant.
Be honest and conservative, a wasted application costs the applicant more than a missed one.

## Applicant
{{ $('Load Profile').first().json.profile_json }}

## Applicant's portfolio site
{{ $('Portfolio Evidence').first().json.portfolio_text }}

## Openings ({{ $json.count }})
{{ $json.openings }}

## How to score
- Return exactly one result per opening, echoing `job_key` verbatim.
- The applicant is an undergraduate still studying. Roles demanding many years of
  experience, or a "senior" / "lead" / "head" / "principal" title, are a poor fit
  however well the technical keywords match, record that in `blockers` and score low.
- A required work permit, mandatory on-site presence in another country, or fluency
  in a language the applicant does not speak is a hard blocker: list it and score
  below 40.
- Reward genuine overlap in tools, domain and demonstrated projects, not job-title
  similarity alone.
- `verdict` must be `skip` whenever `blockers` is non-empty.

parameters.content:
## 4 · Two gates, not one

Scoring decides what is worth **telling** the applicant about.
Blockers decide what may be **submitted**. They are deliberately
separate: a role can be a genuinely good match and still be
un-appliable because it needs a work permit or a language, and the
applicant should hear about it either way rather than have the run
report nothing at all.

## Honest screening, not keyword matching

Gemini scores each opening against the full CV and returns typed
JSON: score, seniority fit, strengths, gaps, hard blockers, and a
one-line summary.

The prompt is deliberately conservative. A student applying to a
"Lead ML Engineer" role scores low no matter how well the keywords
line up, and a required work permit or unfamiliar language is a hard
blocker. A wasted application costs the applicant more than a missed
one does.

## 1 · Your profile lives in the sheet

Fill one row on the **job_profile** tab: name, email, phone, a link to
your CV as a real PDF, target roles, locations, salary and skills.

Every run reads it again, so changing your mind about roles or
salary means editing a cell, not re-running anything. A Google Sheet is
also easier to check and share than a form submission buried in an
execution log.

`profile_json` holds the same values as JSON; that is the column the
prompts actually read.

## 2 · Discover boards, then read them for free

`Find And Shortlist` runs four steps in one node: read the search
hits, fetch every board in parallel, rank locally, and cut the
survivors into batches the model can answer reliably.

`MrScraper → Discovery → Search Google SERP` finds company career
boards. No directory of these subdomains exists, so search is the only
way to enumerate them, the step no API can replace.

Cost: **1 token per query page.**

⚠️ Word order matters: put keywords **before** `site:`.
`data scientist site:recruitee.com` → correct, on-domain results.
`site:recruitee.com data scientist` → the filter is silently dropped.

Openings are then read from the public careers API over plain HTTP:
structured JSON, **zero scraping tokens**. Use the API where one
exists; spend tokens only where none does.

## 3 · Free ranking before paid reasoning

A company board lists *every* vacancy it has, drivers, nurses,
office staff. Sending all of them to an LLM would be slow and
wasteful.

`Find And Shortlist` does this for free inside one node: remote
requirement, a language the applicant actually reads, title keyword
overlap and seniority fit. Only the top few survivors reach a model.

Return null for anything the page does not state, and never invent a number.' : 'Summarise what current and former employees say about working here. parameters.content:
## 5 · The part with no API

Salary figures and employee reviews live on pages that expose no
feed of any kind. `Extract Page by Prompt` reads them and returns
typed JSON, this is where scraping earns its place.

**Extractions are asynchronous.** The node returns a result *id*,
so the Wait → Get Result → IF loop below polls until the status
reads `Finished`. A Code node cannot use a stored credential, so this
is the one place a loop beats a single node.

Salary is cached on role + country, because the market rate for a
role in a country does not change per employer.

parameters.text:
=Prepare one job application on behalf of the applicant below.

## Applicant
{{ $('Load Profile').first().json.profile_json }}

## Applicant's portfolio site, projects and papers the CV leaves out
{{ $('Portfolio Evidence').first().json.portfolio_text }}

## Role
{{ $json.title }} at {{ $json.company }}, {{ $json.location }}
{{ $json.description }}

## Screening questions to answer
{{ JSON.stringify($json.open_questions) }}

## Salary benchmark
{{ JSON.stringify($json.salary_estimate) }}

## Employee reviews
{{ JSON.stringify($json.company_reviews) }}

## How to write
Everything you produce is read by a recruiter and signed with the applicant's
name. Write the way she would write, not the way a model writes.

- **Never use an em dash.** Use a comma, a full stop, or the word "and".
- Short, plain sentences. No sentence should need reading twice.
- Banned openings and phrases: "I am writing to apply", "I am excited to",
  "I am passionate about", "leverage", "delve", "robust", "seamless", "align
  with your mission", "in today's fast-paced", "furthermore", "moreover",
  "it is worth noting", "a testament to".
- Name real things: a project, a number, a tool she actually used. One concrete
  detail beats three sentences of enthusiasm.
- If she lacks something the role asks for, say it plainly in one clause and
  move on. Do not pad around it and do not claim it.
- No bullet points in the cover letter. Three short paragraphs at most.

## Rules, read carefully
1. **Never assert something the evidence does not support.** These answers are
   submitted under the applicant's real name to a real employer. Two sources
   count as evidence: the CV, and the portfolio site above. Check the portfolio
   before concluding she lacks something, since a one-page CV omits most of the
   work. If neither source shows it, she has not done it: say so plainly rather
   than writing around it.
2. For `boolean` questions, set `flag` from the CV alone. If the CV gives no basis
   (a language not listed, a city not lived in, a permit not held), answer `false`
   and set `confident: false`. Never guess `true` to pass a filter.
3. For text questions, answer only from the CV. Say the truth plainly if the
   applicant lacks something; do not pad.
4. For `single_choice`, `content` must be exactly one string from that question's
   own `options` list. For `multi_choice`, join the chosen options with ` | `.
   Never invent an option that is not in the list.
5. Questions asking what the applicant has *done* are factual, answer them from
   the CV with `confident: true` when the CV supports it. Questions testing
   *knowledge of a named tool* the CV never mentions are a quiz for the applicant,
   not for you: pick the option you believe correct but set `confident: false`, so
   the opening is handed back for a human answer rather than submitted.
6. When a question asks about salary expectations, quote `salary_expectation`
   from the applicant profile. Convert the period if the form asks for a
   different one, and never state a bare number without its currency.
7. The cover letter must name something specific about *this* company or role.
   No generic praise, no invented achievements.
8. `salary_verdict`: compare the benchmark to the applicant's stated expectation.
   Write "no data" if the benchmark is null.

parameters.content:
## 6 · Answers the applicant can stand behind

Real screening questions from live boards include *"Are you fluent
in Dutch?"* and *"Do you live within 50 km of Amsterdam?"*, both
marked required.

An LLM optimising for pass-rate would answer yes. This one may only
answer from the CV and must return `confident: false` when it has no
basis.

A hard blocker, permit, language, seniority, drops the opening here.
An unverified answer does not: it is carried to the approval message and
shown to the applicant, who approves only if they stand behind it.

The application is sent under the applicant's real name. A false
answer is not a bug in the workflow, it is a lie to an employer.

## 7 · Nothing is sent without a yes

Openings that clear both gates are not submitted straight away. Each
one is sent to Telegram with its score, pay range, what employees say
and the drafted cover letter, and the workflow **pauses** on
`Send and Wait` until you approve or decline. Approval expires after
12 hours so a run cannot hang forever.

`Send and Wait` can only ask once per execution, so `Apply Loop`
walks the shortlist one opening at a time. **MAX_APPLY** sets how
many rounds it runs; the batch size stays at one because each pass
waits for your answer.

Letters are drafted for `max(MAX_ENRICH, MAX_APPLY)` openings. Only a
drafted opening can be submitted, so capping letters at MAX_ENRICH
alone would quietly make MAX_APPLY unreachable.

This needs a reachable webhook for the button to call back, automatic
on n8n Cloud, and on a local install run n8n with `--tunnel`.

## Submit, or hand over cleanly

Four ATS are searched. Only **Recruitee** publishes an
unauthenticated endpoint for creating a candidate, so only Recruitee
openings are submitted automatically. Lever, Ashby and Greenhouse
publish their listings openly but keep submission behind employer
credentials, those arrive fully researched with the answers drafted,
one tap from done.

`DRY_RUN` (top-left, on by default) runs everything and shows the
exact payload without sending it. Turn it off to submit for real.

Submission is a plain HTTP POST to Recruitee's public careers API, 
no browser automation, no login, no CAPTCHA. It is the same endpoint
the company's own application form posts to.

Every opening is written to the `seen_jobs` table whatever happens,
which is also what stops tomorrow's run from showing it again.
